newsitem.title: ITALY: Europe's "big five" reassure Turkey on EU bid.
newsitem.headline: Europe's "big five" reassure Turkey on EU bid.

text.p: Europe's "Big Five" powers reassured Turkey on Wednesday that there were "no obstacles in principle" to its future membership of the European Union, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said.

But he told reporters that he and colleagues from Britain, Germany, Spain and Italy had also told Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller that Ankara's human rights record and policy on Kurds posed "difficulties" for membership.

De Charette spoke during a break in the informal talks, held to smooth growing strains in Turkey's relations with the European Union and preceded by a threat from Ciller that Ankara could block NATO's enlargement eastwards if its EU ambitions were thwarted.
The French minister said the talks had covered security issues, including NATO expansion, and that discussions on the EU had been "frank and direct and, of course, friendly".

The five EU ministers had raised human rights and the Kurdish question, "which naturally represent difficulties on the path to Turkey's possible membership", as well as Greek-Turkish tensions, De Charette said.
"That said, I had the feeling that the European foreign ministers who took part believed that there weren't any obstacles in principle to Turkey's adhesion in the future," he said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said Turkey's present relationship with the EU was "unsatisfactory".
"We believe Turkey should be treated in the same way as other applicant countries," Rifkind said.

Ciller used a speech on the eve of the meeting to hit home Turkey's frustration at what it considers its "second rate" relationship with the 15-nation EU. She said the matter could no longer be separated from the issue of NATO enlargement.

"The expansion of NATO, the expansion of Europe, they are interlinked," she said on Tuesday night, adding that it "does not make sense" for Turkey to be excluded from EU membership when the bloc is preparing to admit up to 11 other countries.

She made clear that Ankara, a founder member of NATO and key strategic ally of the West, could veto plans by the military alliance to expand into former communist states unless the EU delivered on closer ties.
"How do you think you can expand NATO without Turkey's permission?" Ciller asked.

Diplomats stressed that Wednesday's meeting was informal and no EU decisions could be taken. The talks also addressed increasing strains between EU member Greece and Turkey and efforts to find a solution to the decades-old Cyprus problem.
The search for a settlement has been complicated by Greek Cypriot government plans to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats of military retaliation.

Rifkind said Britain, the former colonial power on the island, regretted the attitude of both sides in the dispute and called for "proper negotiations...this year with a view to major progress" on the island's future.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third of the island after a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by Greece's then ruling military junta.

Diplomats fear that tensions over Cyprus, which hopes to start EU accession talks next year, territorial disputes between Greece and Turkey, and Ankara's EU frustrations could push the Islamist-led government to turn to its Moslem neighbours.
